lessons.title: Homeostasis & the Nervous System
lessons.description: How the body maintains stable internal conditions and how the nervous system detects stimuli and coordinates responses.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Homeostasis?

Your body works best when its internal conditions stay within narrow limits. Homeostasis is the process that keeps factors such as body temperature, blood glucose concentration and water balance at optimal levels. Without homeostasis, enzymes would denature and chemical reactions inside cells would slow down or stop entirely.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains a stable internal environment by controlling conditions such as body temperature, blood glucose concentration and water balance — all of which affect enzyme activity.

All homeostatic control systems involve three key components. A receptor detects a change in the environment (a stimulus). A coordination centre (such as the brain or spinal cord) receives and processes the information. An effector (a muscle or gland) carries out the response to bring the condition back to its set point.

The Nervous System

The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and coordinate behaviour. It uses electrical impulses that travel along nerve cells to produce fast, short-lived responses. The central nervous system (CNS) consists of the brain and the spinal cord. Information from receptors passes along sensory neurones to the CNS, which then sends signals along motor neurones to effectors.

There are three types of neurone you need to know. Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS. Relay neurones are found entirely within the CNS and connect sensory neurones to motor neurones. Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors.

Each neurone has a cell body containing the nucleus, thin fibres called axons and dendrons. The axon is often surrounded by a myelin sheath — a fatty layer that insulates the nerve fibre and speeds up the transmission of impulses.

Synapses

Neurones do not touch each other directly. The tiny gap between two neurones is called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of the first neurone, it triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters. These chemicals diffuse across the synaptic gap and bind to receptors on the membrane of the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. This means signals can only travel in one direction across a synapse.

Key Fact

At a synapse, electrical signals are converted into chemical signals (neurotransmitters) and then back into electrical signals in the next neurone. This ensures impulses travel in one direction only.

The Reflex Arc

A reflex action is an automatic, rapid response to a potentially harmful stimulus. Reflexes protect the body — for example, pulling your hand away from a hot object or your pupil constricting in bright light.

The pathway of a reflex is called a reflex arc. It follows this sequence:

Stimulus → Receptor → Sensory neurone → Relay neurone (in CNS) → Motor neurone → Effector → Response
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For example, if you touch a hot plate, pain receptors in your skin detect the stimulus. The impulse travels along a sensory neurone to a relay neurone in the spinal cord. The relay neurone passes the impulse to a motor neurone, which stimulates the effector (a muscle in your arm) to contract and pull your hand away. This all happens without conscious thought — your brain is not involved in the initial response.

Key Fact

The reflex arc follows the pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response. The brain is bypassed, making the response extremely fast.

Why Homeostasis Matters

The internal environment must stay stable because cells depend on enzyme-controlled reactions. Enzymes have an optimum temperature and pH — if conditions drift too far from the optimum, enzymes change shape (denature) and can no longer catalyse reactions. This is why the body constantly monitors and adjusts conditions using the receptor → coordination centre → effector pathway described above.

Both the nervous system and the endocrine (hormonal) system play roles in homeostasis. The nervous system produces fast, short-term responses via electrical impulses, while the endocrine system produces slower, longer-lasting responses via hormones. You will explore the endocrine system in the next lesson.

In extended-response questions on the nervous system, make sure you describe the full reflex arc pathway in the correct order. A common mistake is to say the brain controls reflex actions — it does not. State clearly that the relay neurone is in the spinal cord and that the response is automatic and involuntary. Use precise terminology: receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Homeostasis is the regulation of internal conditions (temperature, blood glucose, water) to maintain a stable environment for enzyme activity.
  • The nervous system uses electrical impulses along sensory, relay and motor neurones to produce rapid responses. Signals cross synapses via neurotransmitters.
  • Reflex arcs bypass the brain to produce fast, automatic protective responses: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector.

lessons.title: Hormonal Coordination & the Endocrine System
lessons.description: The endocrine system, hormonal glands, hormone production, negative feedback mechanisms, and blood glucose regulation.
lessons.content_html:
The Endocrine System

The endocrine system is a network of glands that produce chemical messengers called hormones. Unlike the nervous system, which uses fast electrical impulses, hormones travel in the blood and produce slower, longer-lasting effects. Hormones are secreted directly into the bloodstream and carried to specific target organs, where they trigger a response.

Key Fact

The main endocrine glands are: the pituitary gland (the "master gland"), thyroid gland, adrenal glands, pancreas, ovaries (in females) and testes (in males). Each gland produces specific hormones that are transported in the blood to target organs.

Key Endocrine Glands and Their Hormones

The pituitary gland, located at the base of the brain, is often called the "master gland" because it secretes hormones that control other endocrine glands. For example, it releases TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) to control the thyroid.

The thyroid gland produces thyroxine, which controls the body's metabolic rate. The adrenal glands, sitting on top of the kidneys, produce adrenaline. The pancreas produces insulin and glucagon to regulate blood glucose. The ovaries produce oestrogen and progesterone, while the testes produce testosterone.

Adrenaline is released by the adrenal glands in response to a stressful or dangerous situation. It prepares the body for "fight or flight" by:

• Increasing heart rate, so more blood is pumped to muscles.
• Raising blood pressure, improving oxygen delivery.
• Increasing blood flow to skeletal muscles, ready for action.
• Stimulating the liver to convert stored glycogen into glucose, raising blood sugar for energy.

Negative Feedback and Thyroxine

Negative feedback is the mechanism by which the body reverses a change to bring conditions back to normal. Thyroxine regulation is a key example you need to understand.

When thyroxine levels drop, the hypothalamus releases TRH (thyrotropin-releasing hormone). TRH stimulates the pituitary gland to release TSH. TSH then acts on the thyroid gland to produce more thyroxine. Once thyroxine levels return to normal, thyroxine inhibits the release of both TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the pituitary — this is the "negative feedback" loop that prevents overproduction.

Key Fact

Thyroxine is controlled by negative feedback: low thyroxine → hypothalamus releases TRH → pituitary releases TSH → thyroid produces thyroxine. When levels are normal, thyroxine inhibits TRH and TSH release.

Blood Glucose Regulation

Blood glucose concentration must be kept within a narrow range. After a meal, blood glucose rises. The pancreas detects this and secretes insulin. Insulin causes cells (especially liver and muscle cells) to absorb glucose from the blood. Excess glucose is converted to glycogen and stored in the liver. This brings blood glucose back down to normal.

When blood glucose falls too low (for example, during exercise), the pancreas releases glucagon. Glucagon stimulates the liver to break down glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood. This is another example of negative feedback — insulin and glucagon work in opposition to keep blood glucose stable.

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the pancreas produces little or no insulin. The body's immune system destroys the insulin-producing cells. It is treated with regular insulin injections and careful monitoring of blood glucose and diet.

Type 2 diabetes occurs when the body's cells no longer respond properly to insulin (insulin resistance) or the pancreas does not produce enough. It is strongly linked to obesity, poor diet and lack of exercise. It can often be controlled through lifestyle changes — a balanced diet, regular exercise and weight loss — though some patients may also need medication.

Doctors use BMI (Body Mass Index) and waist-to-hip ratio to assess the risk of type 2 diabetes. BMI is calculated using: \(\text{BMI} = \frac{\text{mass (kg)}}{\text{height (m)}^2}\). A higher BMI is correlated with a greater risk of developing type 2 diabetes.

Key Fact

Type 1 diabetes — the pancreas produces no insulin (autoimmune); treated with insulin injections. Type 2 diabetes — cells become resistant to insulin; linked to obesity and treated with diet and exercise.

When asked to explain negative feedback, always describe both directions: what happens when the level is too low AND what stops production when the level returns to normal. Many students only describe one direction and lose marks. For blood glucose, make sure you name both hormones (insulin and glucagon) and state they have opposite effects.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood to produce slower, longer-lasting responses than the nervous system.
  • Thyroxine regulation is a key example of negative feedback involving the hypothalamus, pituitary gland and thyroid gland.
  • Blood glucose is controlled by insulin (lowers glucose) and glucagon (raises glucose) from the pancreas. Type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin injections; type 2 is linked to lifestyle and treated with diet and exercise.

lessons.title: Reproduction & Contraception
lessons.description: The menstrual cycle, hormones controlling reproduction, contraception methods, and assisted reproductive technology.
lessons.content_html:
The Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle is a roughly 28-day process controlled by hormones. It prepares the female body for pregnancy each month. If the released egg is not fertilised, the lining of the uterus is shed during menstruation (a period), and the cycle begins again.

The cycle has four main stages. Days 1–5: Menstruation occurs — the uterus lining breaks down and is shed. Days 6–13: The uterus lining begins to rebuild and thicken. Day 14: Ovulation occurs — a mature egg is released from one of the ovaries. Days 15–28: The uterus lining is maintained, ready for a fertilised egg to implant. If no fertilisation occurs, the cycle starts again.

Hormones Controlling the Menstrual Cycle

Four hormones interact to control the menstrual cycle. FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) is released by the pituitary gland. It causes an egg to mature inside a follicle in the ovary and stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen.

Oestrogen is produced by the ovaries. It causes the uterus lining to thicken and repair after menstruation. Rising oestrogen levels also stimulate the pituitary gland to release a surge of LH (luteinising hormone). LH triggers ovulation around day 14.

Key Fact

FSH matures the egg and stimulates oestrogen production. Oestrogen thickens the uterus lining and triggers LH release. LH triggers ovulation. Progesterone maintains the uterus lining after ovulation and inhibits FSH and LH.

After ovulation, the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum and produces progesterone. Progesterone maintains the thick uterus lining so that a fertilised egg can implant. It also inhibits FSH and LH, preventing another egg from maturing. If no fertilisation occurs, the corpus luteum breaks down, progesterone levels drop, and the uterus lining is shed — beginning menstruation and the next cycle.

The hormones of the menstrual cycle interact through feedback loops. Oestrogen produced by the developing follicle stimulates LH release (a positive feedback effect). After ovulation, progesterone from the corpus luteum inhibits both FSH and LH (negative feedback), preventing a second egg from being released. When progesterone falls, FSH is no longer inhibited, so the cycle restarts.

Contraception

Contraception prevents pregnancy. Methods fall into two main categories: hormonal contraception and barrier methods.

Hormonal methods work by releasing hormones that interfere with the menstrual cycle. The combined pill contains oestrogen and progesterone — it prevents ovulation and thickens cervical mucus so sperm cannot pass through easily. The progesterone-only pill (mini-pill) mainly thickens cervical mucus. Other options include contraceptive injections, implants and intrauterine devices (IUDs) that release hormones.

Barrier methods physically block sperm from reaching the egg. Condoms (male and female) also protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Diaphragms cover the cervix and are used with spermicide. Barrier methods have no hormonal side effects but must be used correctly every time.

Hormonal methods are very effective at preventing pregnancy when used correctly but can have side effects such as headaches, mood changes or blood clots. They do not protect against STIs. Barrier methods are less effective at preventing pregnancy but condoms are the only method that protects against STIs. The choice of contraception depends on reliability, side effects, convenience and whether STI protection is needed.

Key Fact

Hormonal contraception is highly effective at preventing pregnancy but does not protect against STIs and can have side effects. Barrier methods (e.g. condoms) protect against STIs but are less effective at preventing pregnancy.

Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART)

Some couples have difficulty conceiving naturally. ART includes treatments that help people become pregnant.

IVF (in vitro fertilisation) involves giving the mother FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs to mature. The eggs are collected and fertilised with sperm in a laboratory. Fertilised embryos develop for a few days before one or two are transferred to the mother’s uterus. IVF is effective but expensive, physically demanding and has a relatively low success rate per cycle.

Clomifene therapy is a fertility drug. It works by stimulating the release of FSH and LH from the pituitary gland, which triggers ovulation. It is less invasive and cheaper than IVF, though it can increase the chance of multiple pregnancies.

Key Fact

IVF involves stimulating egg production with FSH/LH, collecting eggs, fertilising them with sperm in a lab, and transferring embryos to the uterus. Clomifene therapy stimulates ovulation by triggering FSH and LH release.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about the menstrual cycle, draw a quick timeline showing which hormones peak at which stage. Remember that oestrogen stimulates LH (positive feedback), while progesterone inhibits FSH and LH (negative feedback). For contraception evaluation questions, always discuss both advantages and disadvantages of each method.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The menstrual cycle is controlled by four hormones: FSH, oestrogen, LH and progesterone, which interact through feedback loops.
  • Hormonal contraception prevents ovulation or thickens cervical mucus; barrier methods physically block sperm. Condoms are the only method that protects against STIs.
  • ART includes IVF (eggs fertilised in a lab) and clomifene therapy (drug that stimulates ovulation) to help couples who struggle to conceive naturally.

lessons.title: DNA, Genes & Inheritance
lessons.description: The structure of DNA, nucleotides and base pairing, genes and genomes, protein synthesis, and monohybrid inheritance patterns.
lessons.content_html:
The Structure of DNA

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer found in the nucleus of cells. It is shaped as a double helix — two strands twisted around each other like a spiral ladder. Each strand is made up of repeating units called nucleotides.

Each nucleotide consists of three parts: a sugar (deoxyribose), a phosphate group and one of four bases — adenine (A), thymine (T), cytosine (C) or guanine (G). The two strands are linked by complementary base pairs joined by weak hydrogen bonds. Adenine always pairs with thymine (A–T), and cytosine always pairs with guanine (C–G).

Key Fact

A nucleotide = sugar + phosphate + base. The base pairing rules are: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G. The strands are held together by weak hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs.

Genes, Genomes and Protein Synthesis

A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a specific protein. Different proteins control different characteristics. The genome is the entire DNA of an organism — all of its genes and the DNA between them. Understanding the genome helps scientists identify genes linked to diseases and develop new treatments.

Genes are found on chromosomes inside the nucleus. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 in total). Each gene can exist in different versions called alleles, and it is the combination of alleles that determines an organism’s characteristics.

Meiosis is a type of cell division that produces sex cells (gametes) — sperm in males and eggs (ova) in females. Unlike mitosis, meiosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell. These cells are haploid (23 chromosomes in humans).

Because meiosis involves shuffling of genetic material, each gamete is genetically different. When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the resulting zygote has the full set of 46 chromosomes and a unique combination of alleles from both parents.

Monohybrid Inheritance

Inheritance describes how characteristics are passed from parents to offspring through alleles. An allele can be dominant (shown with a capital letter, e.g. B) or recessive (lowercase, e.g. b). A dominant allele is always expressed when present. A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are inherited (one from each parent).

An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is homozygous (BB or bb). An organism with two different alleles is heterozygous (Bb). The combination of alleles is the genotype; the physical characteristic that is expressed is the phenotype.

Key Fact

Dominant alleles are expressed when one or two copies are present. Recessive alleles are only expressed when homozygous (two copies). Genotype = alleles an organism has. Phenotype = the characteristic shown.

A Punnett square is a diagram used to predict the possible outcomes of a genetic cross. You place the alleles from one parent along the top and the alleles from the other parent down the side. Each box shows a possible genotype of the offspring.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
For example, if both parents are heterozygous (Bb × Bb), the Punnett square gives: BB, Bb, Bb, bb. The ratio of phenotypes would be 3 dominant : 1 recessive. This means there is a 75% probability of the dominant phenotype and a 25% probability of the recessive phenotype.

You also need to understand how sex is determined. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), and males have one X and one Y (XY). A Punnett square for sex inheritance shows a 50:50 chance of the offspring being male or female.

Variation

Variation refers to the differences between individuals of the same species. Genetic variation is caused by differences in DNA — these arise through mutations and the mixing of alleles during sexual reproduction (meiosis). Environmental variation results from the conditions an organism lives in, such as diet, sunlight or exercise.

Most characteristics are influenced by both genes and the environment. Most phenotypic features result from multiple genes rather than a single gene. Mutations occur naturally and produce new alleles. Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype. Some have a small effect, and very rarely a single mutation can significantly change the phenotype.

Key Fact

Variation can be genetic (from DNA/alleles), environmental (from surroundings) or both. Most mutations have no effect on phenotype. Most phenotypic features are controlled by multiple genes.

The Human Genome Project

The Human Genome Project was a major international effort to map and sequence every gene in the human genome. Its potential applications include identifying genes linked to inherited diseases, developing personalised medicines, understanding evolutionary relationships between species and advancing forensic science.

When drawing a Punnett square, always show the parental genotypes, the gametes, and the offspring genotypes and phenotypes. State the ratio clearly (e.g. 3:1 or 1:1). A common error is to write the probability as a certainty — say “there is a 25% chance” rather than “one in four offspring will be”. Remember these are probabilities, not guarantees.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • DNA is a double helix of nucleotides with complementary base pairing (A–T, C–G). A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein.
  • Meiosis produces four genetically different haploid gametes. Monohybrid crosses use Punnett squares to predict offspring genotypes and phenotypes.
  • Variation is caused by genetics (mutations, sexual reproduction), the environment, or both. The Human Genome Project mapped all human DNA and has applications in medicine and forensics.

lessons.title: Variation & Evolution
lessons.description: Genetic and environmental variation, natural selection, evolution, and selective breeding in organisms.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Variation?

No two organisms are exactly alike — even identical twins develop small differences over time. The differences between individuals of the same species are called variation. Understanding variation is essential for explaining how evolution works, because natural selection acts on these differences.

Variation can be caused by genetic factors, environmental factors, or usually a combination of both. Genetic variation arises because offspring inherit different combinations of alleles from their parents. Environmental variation is caused by the conditions an organism experiences during its life, such as diet, climate, or injuries.

Key Fact

Genetic variation is caused by differences in DNA (e.g. blood group, eye colour). Environmental variation is caused by an organism’s surroundings (e.g. scars, accent, muscle mass). Most features, like height and weight, are influenced by both.

Sources of Genetic Variation

There are several processes that create genetic variation within a population:

1. Mutations — random changes in the DNA sequence. Most mutations have no effect on the organism, but occasionally a mutation produces a new allele that changes a characteristic. Very rarely, a mutation gives an organism an advantage in its environment.

2. Sexual reproduction — the fusion of gametes from two parents means each offspring inherits a unique combination of alleles. The random mixing of alleles during meiosis and the random fertilisation of gametes both increase variation.

Continuous variation shows a range of values with no clear categories — think of height, mass, or hand span. If you measured the height of every student in a year group and plotted a graph, you would get a smooth bell-shaped curve. Continuous variation is typically controlled by multiple genes and influenced by the environment.

Discontinuous variation falls into distinct categories with no in-between values — blood group (A, B, AB, or O), for example, or whether you can roll your tongue. Discontinuous variation is usually controlled by a single gene with a small number of alleles.

Charles Darwin and Natural Selection

In 1859, Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species, in which he set out his theory of natural selection. Darwin observed that:

1. Individuals within a species show variation in their characteristics. 2. Organisms produce more offspring than the environment can support, so there is competition for resources. 3. Individuals with characteristics best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce — this is sometimes called “survival of the fittest”. 4. These individuals pass on the alleles for their advantageous characteristics to their offspring. 5. Over many generations, the advantageous allele becomes more common in the population, and the species evolves.

Key Fact

Natural selection: Variation → Competition → Survival of the best adapted → Reproduction → Alleles passed on. Over many generations, this changes the characteristics of a population — this is evolution.

Evolution — Change Over Time

Evolution is the gradual change in the inherited characteristics of a population over successive generations. It occurs through natural selection when the environment favours certain traits. Given enough time, natural selection can lead to the development of entirely new species — a process called speciation.

Speciation typically happens when populations of the same species become geographically isolated (separated by a physical barrier such as a mountain range or river). Each group experiences different environmental conditions, so different characteristics are favoured by natural selection. Over a very long time, the two groups become so different that they can no longer interbreed — they have become separate species.

Fossils provide evidence for evolution by showing how organisms have changed over millions of years. The fossil record reveals a progression from simple life forms to more complex ones. Key fossils for human evolution include Ardi (4.4 million years ago), Lucy (3.2 million years ago), and fossils discovered by Richard Leakey (1.6 million years ago). These show a gradual change from ape-like ancestors to modern humans, including changes in skull size, posture, and foot structure.

The development of stone tools over time also provides evidence for human evolution. Early tools were simple and roughly shaped, while later tools became increasingly refined and specialised. Scientists can date stone tools by examining the rock layers and other materials found in the same environment.

The emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria is a modern example that supports Darwin’s theory. When antibiotics are used, most bacteria are killed, but any bacterium with a random mutation that makes it resistant will survive and reproduce. The resistant allele is passed to the next generation. Over time, the whole population becomes resistant. MRSA is a well-known example. This happens within our lifetimes — observable evolution.

Selective Breeding

Selective breeding (also called artificial selection) is when humans deliberately choose which organisms to breed based on desired characteristics. For example, farmers might breed cows that produce the most milk together, or select wheat plants with the highest grain yield. Over many generations, the desired characteristic becomes more pronounced in the population.

Selective breeding has been used for thousands of years to improve food plants (larger fruits, disease resistance, higher yields) and domesticated animals (faster horses, more docile cattle, dogs with specific traits). However, it reduces genetic variation within the bred population, which can cause problems — such as inherited health conditions in pedigree dogs or vulnerability to new diseases in crops with limited genetic diversity.

Key Fact

Natural selection is driven by the environment and takes many generations. Selective breeding is driven by humans choosing which organisms to breed and can produce rapid changes. Both lead to a change in allele frequency in a population.

Edexcel often tests whether you can explain the steps of natural selection using a specific example. Practise writing out the full sequence (variation → competition → survival → reproduction → alleles inherited) applied to a named organism, such as antibiotic-resistant bacteria or peppered moths. Make sure you mention alleles being passed on, not just “traits”.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Variation is caused by genetic factors, environmental factors, or both. Mutations and sexual reproduction create genetic variation.
  • Natural selection acts on variation: organisms best suited to their environment survive, reproduce, and pass on advantageous alleles. Over time, this leads to evolution.
  • Evidence for evolution includes the fossil record (Ardi, Lucy, Leakey fossils), stone tools, and the emergence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

lessons.title: Natural Selection & Classification
lessons.description: Classification systems for organisms, the five kingdoms to three domains shift, and genetic engineering processes.
lessons.content_html:
Classification — Organising the Living World

With millions of species on Earth, scientists need a system to organise and name them. Classification places organisms into groups based on their shared characteristics. Traditionally, organisms were classified into five kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi, protists, and prokaryotes. This system was based mainly on observable features such as body structure and how organisms obtain food.

Key Fact

Modern genetic analysis has led scientists to reclassify life into three domains: Archaea (ancient prokaryotes found in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria), and Eukarya (all organisms with cells containing a nucleus — animals, plants, fungi, and protists). DNA analysis revealed that Archaea are more different from Bacteria than previously thought, so they were separated.

From Five Kingdoms to Three Domains

The five-kingdom system grouped all prokaryotes together. However, when scientists analysed the genome of different prokaryotes, they discovered that Archaea are fundamentally different from Bacteria at the genetic level. Their DNA sequences, cell membrane chemistry, and metabolic processes are distinct. This genetic evidence led to the three-domain system proposed by Carl Woese, which better reflects the evolutionary relationships between organisms.

The third domain, Eukarya, contains all organisms with eukaryotic cells (cells with a nucleus). This domain includes the animal, plant, fungal, and protist kingdoms.

Before DNA technology, classification relied on physical features — what organisms looked like. This sometimes led to mistakes. For example, two organisms might look similar because they adapted to the same environment (convergent evolution), not because they are closely related. Dolphins and sharks look similar but are very different genetically — one is a mammal, the other a fish.

Genetic analysis compares DNA sequences directly. The more similar the DNA of two organisms, the more closely related they are and the more recently they shared a common ancestor. This approach gives a much more accurate picture of evolutionary relationships than physical features alone.

Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering is the process of modifying the genome of an organism to introduce a desirable characteristic. Unlike selective breeding, which takes many generations, genetic engineering can transfer a specific gene from one organism to another in a single step — even between completely different species.

The Main Stages of Genetic Engineering

The process involves four key stages:

1. The desired gene is identified and cut out of the donor organism's DNA using restriction enzymes. These enzymes cut at specific DNA sequences, leaving short, unpaired sections of bases called sticky ends.

2. A vector (such as a bacterial plasmid or a virus) is cut open with the same restriction enzyme, creating matching sticky ends.

3. The desired gene is inserted into the vector. The sticky ends of the gene and the vector are complementary, so they pair up. Ligase enzyme then seals the DNA backbone, joining the gene permanently into the vector.

4. The vector is introduced into the target organism's cells. If successful, the target organism will now produce the protein coded for by the inserted gene, giving it the desired characteristic.

Key Fact

Genetic engineering steps: Cut the gene out with restriction enzymes → Cut the vector with the same enzyme → Insert the gene (sticky ends pair up) → Seal with ligase → Transfer vector to target organism.

Medicine: Human insulin is produced by genetically engineered bacteria. The human insulin gene is inserted into bacterial plasmids, and the bacteria produce large quantities of insulin for people with diabetes. This is more reliable and ethical than extracting insulin from pig or cow pancreases.

Agriculture: Crop plants can be engineered to resist herbicides, pests, or drought. For example, Bt corn contains a gene from a bacterium that produces a natural insecticide, reducing the need for chemical pesticides.

Benefits: Genetic engineering can produce organisms with very specific, useful characteristics quickly. It can improve crop yields, reduce reliance on pesticides, and produce medicines cheaply. Risks and concerns: Genes could transfer to wild populations (gene flow), potentially creating "superweeds". There are ethical concerns about "playing God" and modifying organisms. Long-term effects on ecosystems are not fully understood. Some people are concerned about eating genetically modified (GM) food, although scientific evidence has not shown it to be harmful.

When asked to evaluate genetic engineering, the examiner wants you to give both sides — benefits and risks — and then reach a conclusion. Use specific examples (e.g. insulin production, GM crops) rather than vague statements. Always consider practical, ethical, and environmental implications.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Genetic analysis has replaced the five-kingdom system with three domains: Archaea, Bacteria, and Eukarya, because DNA evidence better reflects evolutionary relationships.
  • Genetic engineering uses restriction enzymes to cut a gene, inserts it into a vector using sticky ends and ligase, then transfers it to a target organism.
  • Genetic engineering has benefits (medicine, agriculture) and risks (gene flow, ethical concerns, unknown long-term effects) that must be evaluated together.

lessons.title: Ecosystems & Biodiversity
lessons.description: How ecosystems are organised, the factors that affect communities, and why biodiversity matters.
lessons.content_html:
Levels of Organisation in an Ecosystem

An ecosystem is a community of living organisms interacting with each other and with the non-living parts of their environment. Ecosystems can be as small as a pond or as large as an ocean. To understand how they work, we organise living things into levels:

Individual → Population → Community → Ecosystem. An individual is a single organism. A population is all the organisms of one species living in the same area. A community is all the different populations living and interacting together. An ecosystem includes the community plus the non-living (abiotic) environment they depend on.

Key Fact

The levels of organisation: Individual → Population (one species, same area) → Community (all species in an area) → Ecosystem (community + abiotic environment).

Abiotic and Biotic Factors

Communities are affected by both living and non-living factors. Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that influence where organisms can survive. Key abiotic factors include:

Temperature — affects the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions and therefore metabolic processes. Most organisms have an optimum range. Light — essential for photosynthesis in plants; affects where plants grow and the animals that depend on them. Water — all organisms need water; availability limits where organisms can live, especially in deserts. Pollutants — chemicals released into the environment can poison organisms or disrupt ecosystems.

Biotic factors are living influences on an ecosystem. The two most important are:

Competition — organisms compete for limited resources. Animals compete for food, water, territory, and mates. Plants compete for light, water, minerals, and space. Predation — the relationship between predators and their prey affects population sizes. If a predator population increases, more prey are eaten, so prey numbers fall. With less food available, predator numbers then decline too, creating cyclical patterns.

Species in a community depend on each other — this is called interdependence. If one species is removed, it can have a knock-on effect throughout the food web. For example, if a pollinating insect declines, the plants it pollinates cannot reproduce, which then affects the animals that eat those plants.

Some organisms have particularly close relationships. In parasitism, one organism (the parasite) benefits at the expense of another (the host). Fleas on a dog and tapeworms in a human gut are examples — the parasite gains food or shelter, while the host is harmed. In mutualism, both organisms benefit. For example, mycorrhizal fungi grow on plant roots — the fungi help the plant absorb mineral ions from the soil, and the plant provides the fungi with sugars from photosynthesis.

Sampling Organisms — Quadrats and Belt Transects

To study the distribution and abundance of organisms in an ecosystem, scientists use sampling techniques. It is not practical to count every individual, so we sample and then estimate the total.

A quadrat is a square frame placed on the ground. You count the organisms inside it. For a reliable estimate, place quadrats randomly (using random number coordinates) and repeat many times. The more quadrats you use, the more reliable your estimate.

A belt transect uses a line (a tape measure) laid across an area. Quadrats are placed at regular intervals along the line. This shows how the distribution of organisms changes across a habitat — for example, from a pond edge into woodland.

Key Fact

To estimate the number of organisms in an area: count the organisms in several quadrats, calculate the mean per quadrat, then multiply by the total area ÷ quadrat area. Formula: $$\text{Estimated population} = \frac{\text{mean count per quadrat} \times \text{total area}}{\text{area of quadrat}}$$

Human Impacts on Biodiversity

Biodiversity is the variety of different species in an ecosystem. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient. However, human activities can both increase and decrease biodiversity.

Fish farming can have negative effects on wild ecosystems. Farmed fish are kept in high densities, which can lead to disease spreading to wild populations. Waste from fish farms pollutes surrounding water, and escaped farmed fish can outcompete native species or interbreed with them, reducing genetic diversity.

Introduction of non-indigenous species (species not native to an area) can devastate local ecosystems. The introduced species may outcompete native organisms for food and habitat, prey on native species, or introduce diseases. For example, grey squirrels introduced to the UK outcompeted the native red squirrel for food and habitat.

Eutrophication occurs when excess nutrients (usually from agricultural fertilisers) wash into rivers and lakes. The nutrients cause rapid growth of algae (an algal bloom). The algae block light to aquatic plants, which die. Bacteria decompose the dead organisms, using up dissolved oxygen. Fish and other aquatic organisms suffocate due to the lack of oxygen.

Maintaining Biodiversity

It is important to maintain biodiversity at both local and global levels. Locally, conservation programmes protect habitats and endangered species. This includes creating nature reserves, protecting hedgerows, and managing woodlands. The conservation of animal species involves breeding programmes, habitat restoration, and legal protection.

Reforestation — replanting trees in deforested areas — has multiple benefits. It restores habitats for wildlife, absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere (reducing the greenhouse effect), prevents soil erosion, and increases biodiversity. Globally, international agreements and conservation organisations work to protect endangered species and critical habitats such as rainforests, coral reefs, and wetlands.

Key Fact

Humans reduce biodiversity through fish farming, introducing non-indigenous species, and eutrophication. We can maintain biodiversity through conservation (protecting species and habitats) and reforestation (planting trees to restore ecosystems and absorb CO₂).

Fieldwork questions often ask you to describe a method and explain why certain steps improve reliability. Remember: random placement of quadrats avoids bias, repeating measurements improves reliability, and using a belt transect shows how distribution changes across a habitat. Always state the specific measurements you would take.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ecosystems are organised into individuals, populations, communities, and the whole ecosystem. Abiotic factors (temperature, light, water, pollutants) and biotic factors (competition, predation) affect communities.
  • Quadrats and belt transects are used to sample organisms and estimate population size. Random sampling and large sample sizes improve reliability.
  • Human activities (fish farming, non-indigenous species, eutrophication) can reduce biodiversity. Conservation and reforestation help maintain it.

lessons.title: Trophic Levels, Pyramids & the Carbon Cycle
lessons.description: How the carbon, water, and nitrogen cycles recycle essential materials through ecosystems.
lessons.content_html:
Trophic Levels and Food Chains

In any ecosystem, energy flows from the Sun through living organisms. The position an organism occupies in a food chain is called its trophic level. Every food chain begins with a producer — an organism (usually a green plant or alga) that converts light energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis.

Organisms that eat producers are called primary consumers (trophic level 2). Those that eat primary consumers are secondary consumers (trophic level 3). Tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers and sit at trophic level 4 or above.

Key Fact

Trophic levels: Level 1 = Producers (plants) → Level 2 = Primary consumers (herbivores) → Level 3 = Secondary consumers (carnivores) → Level 4 = Tertiary consumers (top predators). Energy is transferred along the chain but decreases at each level.

Pyramids of Biomass

A pyramid of biomass represents the total mass of living material at each trophic level. The producer level always forms the widest bar at the bottom, and each successive level is narrower. This is because energy is lost at every trophic level, so less biomass can be supported higher up the food chain.

Energy is lost between trophic levels through several processes: organisms use energy for movement and other life processes; energy is lost as heat during respiration; and not all parts of an organism are eaten (bones, shells, roots). As a result, only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed to the next.

Unlike pyramids of numbers (which can sometimes be inverted, for example when a single large tree supports many insects), pyramids of biomass are almost always a true pyramid shape. This is because they show the total mass of organisms, not just how many there are. Since energy is lost at each transfer, the total biomass decreases at each trophic level, regardless of the number or size of individual organisms.

This also explains why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels — by the fifth level, so little energy remains that it cannot support a viable population of top predators.

Material Cycles — Why Recycling Matters

The materials that living organisms are made from are constantly recycled between the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts of an ecosystem. When organisms die, decomposers (mainly bacteria and fungi) break down the dead material. This releases nutrients back into the soil and gases back into the atmosphere, where they can be used again by other organisms. Without decomposition, essential elements would remain locked up in dead organisms and would eventually run out.

The Carbon Cycle

The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, and the environment. It is one of the most important material cycles because carbon is the basis of all organic molecules.

The key processes in the carbon cycle are:

Photosynthesis — producers remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and convert it into glucose (organic compounds). This is the main way carbon enters living systems.

Respiration — all living organisms (plants, animals, and microorganisms) carry out respiration, releasing carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. The equation: $$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

Feeding — carbon passes along food chains when animals eat plants or other animals.

Decomposition — when organisms die, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the organic matter. The decomposers respire, returning carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. This is a critical role of microorganisms in the carbon cycle.

Combustion — burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) releases carbon dioxide that was locked away millions of years ago, increasing atmospheric CO₂ levels.

Key Fact

Carbon enters living systems through photosynthesis and returns to the atmosphere through respiration, decomposition, and combustion. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) play a vital role by breaking down dead matter and respiring, returning carbon to the cycle.

The Water Cycle

The water cycle describes how water moves continuously between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere. The main processes are: Evaporation — water from oceans, lakes, and rivers is heated by the Sun and turns into water vapour. Transpiration — plants release water vapour from their leaves. Condensation — water vapour cools as it rises and condenses into tiny droplets, forming clouds. Precipitation — water falls as rain, snow, or hail. The water then collects in rivers, lakes, and oceans, or soaks into the ground.

In areas of drought, potable water (safe drinking water) can be produced by desalination — removing salt from seawater. This can be done by distillation (boiling and condensing) or reverse osmosis (forcing water through a membrane). Desalination is effective but requires a lot of energy, making it expensive.

Plants need nitrates from the soil to make amino acids and proteins. But plants cannot use nitrogen gas (N₂) directly from the atmosphere. Nitrates are made available to plants in three main ways:

1. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria — these live freely in the soil or in root nodules of leguminous plants (peas, beans, clover). They convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia, which is then converted to nitrates by other bacteria. 2. Decomposition and nitrifying bacteria — when organisms die, decomposers break down proteins into ammonia. Nitrifying bacteria then convert ammonia into nitrites and then into nitrates that plants can absorb. 3. Fertilisers — farmers add artificial fertilisers containing nitrates directly to the soil. Crop rotation with leguminous plants also helps — the nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules enrich the soil with nitrates for the next crop.

Denitrifying bacteria do the reverse — they convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, which is released into the atmosphere. This completes the cycle but can reduce soil fertility.

Key Fact

Nitrates are made available for plants through: 1. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (in soil or legume root nodules). 2. Decomposers + nitrifying bacteria converting dead matter → ammonia → nitrates. 3. Adding fertilisers or using crop rotation with legumes.

When describing the carbon cycle, always mention the role of microorganisms as decomposers. Decomposers don't just break things down; they also respire, which is what actually returns carbon dioxide to the atmosphere. Many students forget this second step. Also remember that combustion of fossil fuels is a human addition to the cycle that increases atmospheric CO₂.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Trophic levels show an organism’s position in a food chain. Energy is lost at each level (as heat, movement, and waste), so biomass decreases — giving pyramids their characteristic shape.
  • The carbon cycle: photosynthesis removes CO₂, while respiration, decomposition, and combustion return it. Microorganisms are essential decomposers.
  • Nitrates reach plants via nitrogen-fixing bacteria, nitrifying bacteria acting on decomposed matter, and artificial fertilisers or crop rotation.
